name: Photo comparison / flip test

lead: The flip test means comparing your photo with a horizontally flipped copy, or with your mirror image, to understand why you look different in pictures and which version looks better.

The chain: compare the versions, notice which side or look is more flattering, then choose angles and framing accordingly. Users say familiarity with the mirror image shapes preference, which relates to the mere-exposure effect, first studied by Zajonc in 1968. No studies have tested the practice itself.

paras: People flip selfies in a photo app, view them beside the originals and pick the version or angle they prefer for profiles and posts. It takes minutes and is often repeated across several photos.
No physical risks. Some community members report distress from close self-scrutiny.

web.title: Left-Right Facial Orientation of Familiar Faces

chain: Spot which side or version looks better
angle.text: Users flip photos or compare them with their mirror image to understand why they look different in pictures and to pick the more flattering version and angle. It relates to the mere-exposure effect, though the method itself has not been tested.

lead: The photo comparison or flip test is a looksmaxxing practice in which a person compares photos of themselves with the mirror-reversed version of the same photo, or with their mirror reflection, to understand why they look different in pictures than in the mirror and to judge which version they look best in. People use it to assess symmetry, find their better side and choose which photos or angles present their face most favourably.

Related published research exists. In a 2010 Frontiers in Psychology study (Amestoy, Bouvard and Cazalets), about 71 percent of adults preferred the mirror image of their own face, while 76 to 84 percent preferred the standard orientation of a friend's face; the authors linked this to the mere-exposure hypothesis, since people mostly see themselves reversed in mirrors.[1] The effect was first reported in a 1977 study by Mita, Dermer and Knight.[1]

The mere-exposure effect, in which repeated exposure to a stimulus increases liking, was first studied by Zajonc in 1968,[2] and reference works describe facial symmetry as one factor in perceived attractiveness.[3]

paras: A mirror shows a face reversed left to right, while a photo and other people see it the standard way. In the flip test, a person looks at a photo and its horizontally flipped copy side by side, or at both a mirror and a photo, and notes which looks better and where differences appear.

The mere-exposure effect holds that familiarity increases liking; Bornstein's 1989 meta-analysis of 208 experiments found r = 0.26.[2] Proponents of the flip test say people prefer their mirrored face because it is the one they see most.

Research directly tests this. A 1977 paper by Mita, Dermer and Knight, 'Reversed facial images and the mere-exposure hypothesis', is cited as finding that people preferred mirror-reversed versions of their own faces while close friends preferred the normal photographs.[1] The 2010 study by Amestoy and colleagues repeated the design in 38 adults and 72 children aged 3 to 12; preference patterns appeared in children from about 5 to 7 years, and a control group viewing unfamiliar faces showed no preference between orientations.[1]
Facial symmetry research is reported to link symmetry with perceived attractiveness, which is one reason communities compare original and flipped images.[3]
Community members use flips and side-by-side comparisons to evaluate symmetry, jaw and other features, and some say photos show how others see them.
No studies found of the flip test as a self-improvement practice. Related laboratory studies of mirror-image preference are described above.[1]

timeline.event: Zajonc begins studying the mere-exposure effect.[2]
Mita, Dermer and Knight report preference for mirror-reversed images of one's own face.[1]
Amestoy, Bouvard and Cazalets study the preference in children and adults.[1]
